# LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environments via Modular Recombination

Zhuosong Jiang    Chengxu Wu    Junqi Liu    Yujie Yi    Siqin Wang   
Zhixuan Huang    Jinqian Jiang    Lijun Xiao    Jianxun Li    Yongyang
Pan    Jieran Wang    Shiqi Shen    Fei Liu Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao
Tong University  Tencent  Emory University    Xinyu Lin
Affiliation: National University of Singapore  Peking University
 University of California, Santa Cruz

###### Abstract

LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet existing
environments are designed for specific tasks and fail to generalize to
new ones. Recent methods automate environment construction with LLMs.
However, they generate each environment from scratch, neither reusing
parts shared across environments nor carrying a fix from one environment
to the rest. To address this, we propose a new paradigm of _evolving
environment atoms_, which composes environments from reusable atoms
(intent, rule, data and server) and evolves the atoms when an
environment fails to give reliable feedback (e.g., an application lacks
a tool the task requires). To instantiate this paradigm, we introduce
LegoEnv, which builds 5,465 verified environments over 223 applications,
and one round of evolution raises the share of solvable environments
from 71.6% to 88.3%. On AutomationBench, SFT on these environments lifts
Qwen3.6-27B from 16.0% to 32.0%, and RL with their verifiers lifts
Qwen3.8-27B from 37.6% to 40.3%. Further analyses show steady gains with
corpus size, transfer to unseen applications, and failures concentrated
in a few shared root causes.

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range
of domains, spanning from resolving complex issues in software
engineering ([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib40); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39)) and solving competition mathematics ([DeepSeek-AI,
2025](#bib.bib36)) to discovering new knowledge and algorithms ([Lu et
al., 2024](#bib.bib43); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)). Agents
acquire these abilities by interacting with environments, where the
agent acts, the environment responds, and the response becomes
supervision, as trajectories for supervised fine-tuning ([Zeng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib32); [Prabhakar et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10); [Pan et al., 2024](#bib.bib47)) or rewards for
reinforcement learning ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib36); [Qian et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Dong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Da et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)). Since an agent can learn only what its environments
can pose and check, the construction and quality of environments are
among the most critical steps in agent training.

Figure 1: Overview of LegoEnv. Four pools of atoms are collected from
real sources and composed into skeletons under structural constraints. A
builder agent turns each skeleton into an environment, which is admitted
only after its verifier passes a correctness check. Environments that
yield no successful trajectory are diagnosed, and the result files an
issue against an atom and waits for its fix, supplements a pool, or
revises the builder; tasks that are merely hard are kept.

Existing environments are typically designed for a specific task, with
the data, the tools and the verifier built together to provide
high-quality feedback ([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib44); [Xie et al.,
2024](#bib.bib42); [Yao et al., 2024](#bib.bib45); [Trivedi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib46); [Shepard and Salimans, 2026](#bib.bib1); [Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)).¹¹ 1 We count one environment per concrete task,
together with the applications, data and verifier it requires. For
example, paying the approved invoices of a month is one environment, and
escalating the overdue invoices on the same applications is another.
However, they fail to generalize when the task becomes more complex or
moves to a new scenario (e.g., an office agent’s task shifts from paying
invoices in an accounting system to onboarding employees in an HR
system), since different tasks require different data, tools, operations
and checks. Therefore, scalable construction that quickly builds
high-quality environments for diverse tasks is essential for training
agents effectively and efficiently.

To scale environments up, recent methods use LLMs to generate the tools,
data and tasks of each environment ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11);
[Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Tu et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Wang et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib5); [Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib3); [Zeng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37); [Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)). However, different
environments share common parts (e.g., a mail application for sign-off
and an approval policy) while differing in task-specific ones (e.g.,
invoice records versus employee profiles). Generating each environment
from scratch thus neither reuses the experience gained from previous
constructions nor avoids the cost of rebuilding the shared parts
(Table [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

Based on the above insights, we propose a new paradigm, _evolving atoms_
for scalable agentic environments, which builds environments from
smaller reusable units. Specifically, we decompose an environment into
four kinds of atoms, namely intent (goal to achieve), rule (business
rule to follow), data (records for the agent to use), and server (tool
provider), and construct each environment by composing them. When an
environment fails, we trace the failure to the atoms behind it and
evolve those atoms, so that every later environment built from them
benefits. This paradigm brings three benefits. (1) Scalability. New
environments are created by composing existing atoms, so their number
grows with the compositions rather than with manual effort. (2)
Self-evolution. Atom sets and atom properties will be evolved from
construction failures, therefore allowing later environments to avoid
the same errors and reuse the new atoms. (3) Real-world grounding. Every
atom is initially collected from a real source, so the environments
reflect real-world needs and carry practical value.

Based on this paradigm, we develop LegoEnv
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
for business domains. LegoEnv first collects atoms from real sources and
recombines them under structural constraints. It then builds an
environment from each valid composition and keeps it only if its
verifier passes a correctness test. Finally, it diagnoses the
environments that no teacher can solve and evolves the atoms that cause
the failures, which raises the share of solvable environments from 71.6%
to 88.3% in one round. We evaluate LegoEnv on AutomationBench ([Shepard
and Salimans, 2026](#bib.bib1)), MCP-Mark ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2))
and BFCL v4 ([Patil et al., 2025](#bib.bib31)). Supervised fine-tuning
on our environments improves Qwen3.6-27B by 100% and Qwen3.5-27B by 625%
on AutomationBench, outperforming four public synthesis pipelines by 37%
to 87% under the same budget. Using the environments’ verifiers as
rewards for reinforcement learning further improves Qwen3.8-27B by 7.2%.

Our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We propose _evolving atoms_, a paradigm that composes environments
  from reusable intent, rule, data, and server atoms, which are
  collected from real sources and evolve over time.
- •
  We instantiate it as LegoEnv, which tests every verifier before use
  and attributes each environment fault to an atom, a verifier kind or a
  builder instruction, so that one repair reaches every environment that
  shares it.
- •
  We show that the environments improve three bases on AutomationBench,
  with supervised gains that transfer to MCP-Mark, exceed four public
  pipelines at equal budget, and serve unchanged as rewards for
  reinforcement learning.

## 2 Related Work

##### Environment Construction.

Building high-quality environments is an essential step for agent
learning. One line of work builds scalable environments for specific
scenarios, such as web ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib22); [Xiao et al., 2026](#bib.bib26)), computer
use ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)),
terminal ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib17); [Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib29)) and software engineering ([Guo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)), or within one ecosystem ([Nex-AGI Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)), so each new scenario requires redesigning the
synthesis rules by hand. To generalize across scenarios, recent
pipelines automate construction with LLMs: they generate servers from
API definitions ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)), website names ([Wang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib5)) or domain names ([Tu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)), records from schemas or fictitious seeds ([Song et
al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib5); [Tu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)), and tasks from tool graphs or dependencies ([Fang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib11); [Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib3)), and they link
applications by parameter similarity, retrieval or database merging ([Xu
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib3); [Xi et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Sun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)). However, they generate each environment from scratch,
so shared parts are rebuilt every time and a fix in one environment
never reaches the others. To enable automatic environment construction
across tasks, [Yang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib38) reuse a library of
services, but the library remains fixed when generating environments. In
contrast, LegoEnv composes environments from reusable intent, rule, data
and server atoms collected from real sources, and evolves these atoms
when environments fail, so every later environment inherits the fix
(Table [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"),
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

##### Environment Verification.

Existing pipelines decide whether an agent completes a task with an LLM
judge, alone or with rules ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib5); [Dong et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Xi et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Xu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib14); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), or by comparing
final states ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11); [Tu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7); [Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib3); [Cai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)), assuming the verifier itself is correct; a wrong
verifier silently rewards wrong behavior. [Zhang et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib15) repair synthetic web environments, but only to make
tasks solvable. In contrast, LegoEnv tests each verifier before use: it
must fail on the initial world and pass on the reference solution, or
its environment is discarded.

##### Environment Evolution.

To constantly give reliable feedback across tasks on different agents,
environment evolution has become a promising solution. Some work evolves
what is asked: [Dong et al. (2026)](#bib.bib4) generate tasks where the
current policy fails, and [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27) and [Liu et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib16) co-evolve a task generator with the learner.
Alternatively, some work fixes errors by repairing each failed
environment individually ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Zhang et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib15)). In contrast, LegoEnv traces each failure to a
verifier defect, a world defect, or task difficulty, and repairs the
shared atoms or composition vocabulary behind it, so every environment
built from them inherits the fix
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Rollouts and self-evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

## 3 Method

In this section, we first introduce two key basic components in LegoEnv,
_i.e.,_ shared condition form
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Shared condition form ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
for environment evolution; and atoms
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Atoms ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")),
the basic unit for environment construction. Based on the components,
LegoEnv builds each environment through three progressive checks. First,
atoms are composed into a skeleton, which is dropped if the atoms are
incompatible
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
Second, a builder turns the skeleton into an environment, and revises it
until its verifier passes a correctness test
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
Third, a teacher attempts the task; if every attempt fails, a diagnosis
agent finds the cause and either repairs an atom, revises the builder,
supplements a pool, or keeps the task as a hard one
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Rollouts and self-evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
shows the loop and
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Atoms ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
illustrates the atoms and the constraints between them.

### 3.1 Shared condition form

To build LegoEnv and achieve the three progressive checks, we first
introduce a shared condition form. A condition is a triple
$`\langle e,\varphi,\kappa\rangle`$: an entity $`e`$, a scope
$`\varphi`$, which is a conjunction of comparisons on the columns of
$`e`$, and a cardinality $`\kappa`$. It holds when the number of rows of
$`e`$ that satisfy $`\varphi`$ meets $`\kappa`$. For example, a server
lets an invoice be paid only if it has been approved:
$`e=\mathtt{Approval}`$,
$`\varphi=\{\mathtt{invoice}=\mathtt{\$arg.id},\ \mathtt{status}=\mathtt{approved}\}`$,
$`\kappa\geq 1`$. A verifier asserts, in the same form, that no overdue
payable was left unescalated: $`e=\mathtt{Payable}`$,
$`\varphi=\{\mathtt{due}<\mathtt{\$now},\ \mathtt{escalated}=\mathtt{false}\}`$,
$`\kappa=0`$. The conditions a server checks before running a tool, the
constraints on its tables, and the assertions of a verifier are all
written in this one form and evaluated by one evaluator. A verifier can
therefore say exactly what a server can check, no more and no less.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A The condition form ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
gives the full grammar.

### 3.2 Atoms

Figure 2: The four atom pools on one worked example (pay invoices over
10,000 only if approved). The brown links, numbered 1–4, are the four
structural constraints of
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination").

Each atom is collected once from a real source and reused.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Atom schemas ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
gives the schema and a real instance of each.

##### Server atoms.

A server atom is one application, compiled from its open-source code:
its entities, the tools that operate on them, the condition each tool
checks before it runs, and the message the tool returns when the
condition fails, which is what the agent sees when it hits a wall. From
467 open-source repositories we obtain 384 usable servers
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Compiling a server atom ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"));
the environments in this paper use 223 of them.

##### Data atoms.

A data atom is a public dataset with a card that records which tables
have enough rows, the type of each column, and which kinds of rule the
columns can support: a threshold needs a numeric column, a deadline a
date. Worlds are seeded from these datasets, never from generated
records. Of 336 datasets, 281 have a usable table.

##### Intent atoms.

An intent atom specifies a single write that must, or must not, happen
on a server. It is defined by an _operation kind_, a recurring class of
write across applications such as _create invoice_ or _post message_;
each server’s card says which of its tools implement which kinds.
Whether an intent was fulfilled is checked by one or more _verifier
kinds_, templates over the condition form of
§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Shared condition form ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
such as _mail sent with terms_ or _row cell equals_; the verifier kinds
were grounded in public documentation of business workflows
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Inducing the verifier kinds ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
Across our corpus, the vocabulary covers 110 operation kinds and 45
verifier kinds. The vocabulary is not fixed: it expands whenever new
servers introduce write operations that no kind yet expresses
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Rollouts and self-evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
An operation kind can _carry a rule_ if its verifier kinds can tell
valid records from invalid ones.

##### Rule atoms.

A rule atom is a business rule the agent has to find and follow: an
_archetype_, the kind of rule it is (threshold routing, exclusion,
deadline escalation, tiering, approval chain, budget quota,
reconciliation, compliance flag), a shape free of names and numbers, an
_optional exception_ that overrides the rule for some records (_unless
marked urgent_, _unless approved by a manager_), and a _carrier_, the
place in the world that holds the rule’s text, such as a policy
worksheet, a document, a mail or a note on a record. The request names
the carrier and never restates the rule.

### 3.3 Structural atom recombination

The collected atoms of the four families form the _atom pool_, and the
closed sets of names they draw on, the operation kinds, verifier kinds,
archetypes and carriers of
§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Atoms ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"),
form the _vocabulary_ $`\mathcal{V}`$. A skeleton $`\sigma=(S,I,r,d)`$
picks from the pool a candidate workflow
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")):
up to six servers $`S`$, the intent atoms $`I`$, a rule atom $`r`$ and a
dataset $`d`$. Its parts must satisfy four structural constraints:

- •
  Tool coverage. Every intent’s operation kind is implemented by a tool
  of its server in $`S`$.
- •
  Carrier hosting. Some server in $`S`$ hosts the carrier of $`r`$.
- •
  Schema compatibility. $`d`$ supports the archetype of $`r`$.
- •
  Rule attachment. Some intent in $`I`$ carries $`r`$.

A validator enforces tool coverage and carrier hosting on the skeleton.
Schema compatibility is checked against the dataset card while the
environment is built, and rule attachment is a requirement placed on the
builder
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"));
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Every stage on the builder model ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
measures how often random compositions satisfy each.

Figure 3: Structural recombination. A seed skeleton $`\sigma`$ mined
from a procedure is edited by replacing an intent
($`i_{8}\rightarrow i_{12}`$), replacing the rule or adding an atom; the
candidate is kept only if constraints 1–4 of
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Atoms ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
all hold, and duplicates are removed.

##### Seed mining.

These constraints make uniform sampling from the atom pool inefficient:
of 10,000 skeletons assembled at random from the pool, with kinds drawn
from those each server implements, 13–14% satisfy all four constraints
(1.6–1.7% if every intent must carry the rule), and with the rule atom
removed all 10,000 pass
(Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Every stage on the builder model ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
We therefore mine seed skeletons from real workflow descriptions. Given
a business domain $`D`$ and the atom vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$, which
fixes the valid operation kinds, verifier kinds, archetypes and
carriers, a mining agent reads public automation templates and operating
procedures
(Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M Sources ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")),
maps each step onto $`\mathcal{V}`$, and writes one skeleton per
workflow together with the page it came from:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathrm{Mine}(D,\mathcal{V})\longrightarrow\sigma_{\mathrm{seed}}=(S,I,r,d).
``` |  |

The validator checks each $`\sigma_{\mathrm{seed}}`$ and returns the
violated constraint to the agent, which revises the skeleton until it is
accepted. This produced 1,394 seed skeletons.

##### Recombination.

Seeds are then edited within their domain: an intent atom is replaced,
the rule atom is replaced, or an atom is added, with the rest of the
skeleton held fixed; the result must again pass the validator, and
duplicates are removed. Recombination produced 3,400 further skeletons.

### 3.4 Building and admission

A builder agent (brief in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Prompts ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
turns $`\sigma`$ into an environment $`E=(W_{0},q,V,\pi)`$: an initial
world $`W_{0}`$ seeded from $`d`$, with the rule’s text in its carrier
and distractor records that satisfy the rule in all but one clause; a
request $`q`$; a verifier $`V=V^{+}\cup V^{-}`$, positive assertions for
what must be written and negative ones for what must be left untouched;
and a reference solution $`\pi`$, a sequence of tool calls. The builder
runs its program, reads the errors and revises until $`E`$ passes the
*verifier correctness check* below and is admitted.

Write $`W_{\pi}=\pi(W_{0})`$ for the world after the reference solution
and $`\pi\setminus s`$ for $`\pi`$ with one write step $`s`$ removed.
$`E`$ is admitted when

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\forall a\in V^{+}\!:\ \neg a(W_{0}),\quad\forall a\in V^{-}\!:\ a(W_{0});`$ |  | (1) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\forall a\in V:\ a(W_{\pi});`$ |  | (2) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\forall a\in V^{+}\ \ \exists s\in\pi:\ \neg a\big((\pi\setminus s)(W_{0})\big);`$ |  | (3) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\forall a\in V^{-}\ \ \exists W^{\prime}:\ \neg a(W^{\prime});`$ |  | (4) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{reset}(W_{\pi})=W_{0}.`$ |  | (5) |

Conditions
([1](#S3.E1 "In 3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
and
([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
exclude a verifier that is already satisfied or that nothing can
satisfy;
([3](#S3.E3 "In 3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
and
([4](#S3.E4 "In 3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
exclude assertions that test nothing;
([5](#S3.E5 "In 3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
makes every attempt start from the same world. An admitted $`E`$ makes a
later failure informative: if $`\pi`$ passes and a capable agent does
not, the fault is in the task or in the agent, and $`V`$ says which,
unless $`V`$ itself over-specifies the request
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 One round of evolution ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

### 3.5 Rollouts and self-evolution

To test whether an admitted environment can be solved, a teacher agent
attempts it $`N=8`$ times. Trajectories that $`V`$ accepts enter the
supervised corpus, and $`V`$ itself is the reward for reinforcement
learning
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 The same verifiers as a reward ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

When an environment yields no successful trajectory, a *diagnosis agent*
reads $`E`$, the reference solution $`\pi`$ and the failed trajectories
to find the cause, and one of four pathways follows, the four return
arrows of
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"):

- •
  Repair an atom. An atom is at fault, for example a server lacks the
  tool for a required write. An issue is filed against the atom and its
  patch reaches every later environment built from it.
- •
  Revise the builder. $`V`$ demands something that neither $`q`$ nor
  $`r`$ states, or a verifier kind is read two ways. The builder’s
  instructions or the vocabulary are revised, not one environment.
- •
  Supplement the pool. The failure exposes a missing capability. A
  server, an operation kind or a dataset is added to the atom pool.
- •
  Keep as a hard task. The environment is sound and the teacher cannot
  solve it. It is kept unchanged as a hard task.

Through this loop both the atoms and the vocabulary for composing them
evolve from round to round
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")b).

Mining, building, diagnosis, repair and onboarding are all done by
agents;
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Every stage on the builder model ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
runs each stage on the model that builds the environments.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setup

Figure 4: (a) AutomationBench pass rate as the corpus grows. Qwen3.6-27B
rises to 34.8% and Qwen3.5-27B to 26.3%. Bands are evolution rounds. (b)
What each round adds; brown marks a value that grew, grey repeats the
previous value. Operation kinds are counted under the final taxonomy and
rule archetypes are the closed vocabulary introduced in round 2
(Appendix [L](#A12 "Appendix L Repair examples ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

##### Evaluation.

We evaluate on AutomationBench ([Shepard and Salimans,
2026](#bib.bib1)), 600 cross-application business workflows over
simulated SaaS applications that share no application with our
environments
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Overlap with AutomationBench ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"));
MCP-Mark ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)), 127 tasks over five MCP
servers, none among our atoms; and BFCL v4 ([Patil et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31)), seven function-calling categories including
*Irrelevance*, declining a call that should not be made. We run all
three under one protocol
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

##### Models.

We train three base models of the same 27B family, a weak, a mid and a
strong starting point: their zero-shot scores on AutomationBench are
3.2%, 16.0% and 37.6%, against 51.2% for the strongest system we
measured, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Qwen3.8-27B also serves as the teacher: every supervised trajectory is
sampled from it, so the supervised results on Qwen3.5-27B and
Qwen3.6-27B are distillation from a 37.6% model, not from a stronger
external one.

##### Corpora.

The corpus grew over the evolution rounds of
§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Rollouts and self-evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"),
and each round’s corpus contains the previous one
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")b):
round 0 covers the environments that can be built on the unrepaired
server atoms, round 1 adds those the server repairs made buildable,
round 2 adds the environments built from skeletons that carry a rule
atom, a family every environment has from this round on, and round 3
adds the repaired environments. Between rounds 1 and 2 we also draw 1k,
2k and 3k of the round-2 additions, stratified by mining batch. The
teacher rolls out every environment eight times, a trajectory is kept
only if the verifier accepts the final world, and every corpus keeps at
most three trajectories per environment, so all points lie on one scale.
The round-2 corpus spans 223 applications, 99.5% of its trajectories
cross two or more, and
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Corpus profile ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
profiles it.

### 4.2 Main results

Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
compares each base with its trained checkpoint on the three suites;
every base improves on AutomationBench, the two SFT bases on MCP-Mark,
and the two stronger bases on BFCL v4.

##### Imitation.

The gains on AutomationBench are largest for the two weaker bases:
Qwen3.5-27B goes from 3.2% to 23.2% and Qwen3.6-27B from 16.0% to 32.0%.
Per task, Qwen3.5-27B wins 129 and loses 9 against its base, and
Qwen3.6-27B wins 127 and loses 30.

##### Reward.

Qwen3.8-27B is the teacher, so imitation alone is not expected to
improve it; the verifiers of the environments, written by
DeepSeek-V4-Flash ([DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)) when it built
them, can. Used unchanged as a binary reward for GRPO, these verifiers
move Qwen3.8-27B from 37.6% to 40.3% (two evaluations each; 65:53 and
78:58 wins to losses per task), a modest gain on a base that already
scores well above DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the model that wrote the verifiers,
at 32.3%.

##### Transfer.

On MCP-Mark, none of whose servers is among our atoms, Qwen3.5-27B gains
15.1 points and Qwen3.6-27B 26.0; on BFCL v4, Qwen3.6-27B gains 9.4 on
the official average, most of it on *Search* (27.9 to 67.5), where its
base score was an outlier. Two BFCL categories move the other way, its
*Irrelevance* and Qwen3.5-27B’s multi-turn score, and Qwen3.8-27B’s
MCP-Mark gain is within noise
(§[5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 What the training does not buy ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

## 5 Analysis

### 5.1 Scaling the atom pool

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")a
varies the number of trajectories, and both bases improve as the corpus
grows: Qwen3.6-27B rises from 16.0% to about 35%, the last four points
within three points of one another; Qwen3.5-27B rises from 3.2% to
26.3%, with one dip of half a point.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")b
shows what each round added.

### 5.2 One round of evolution

Of the 4,662 environments admitted in round 2 (built from 4,794
skeletons), 71.6% yield at least one accepted trajectory in eight
teacher attempts; we call this fraction the *yield*. The 1,324 that
yield nothing look no different from the rest: they passed admission and
read as reasonable tasks, so a judge-based pipeline would discard them.
Admission
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Building and admission ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
rejects a vacuous or already-satisfied verifier; one that demands a
value the request never states passes, because the reference solution
carries it, and only a rollout exposes it.

With an executable verifier and a reference solution the fault can be
located, and it is of three kinds. Half (52%) are verifier faults: the
verifier demands something neither the request nor the rule asked for. A
quarter (23%) are world faults: a record, a column or a tool the task
needs is missing or inconsistent. The rest (25%) are sound environments
the teacher cannot solve. Repairing the first two kinds and re-sampling
lifts the yield from 71.6% to 88.3%; the third kind is left unchanged.
After re-sampling, 220 of the repaired environments still yield nothing
and form the exploration set of
§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 The same verifiers as a reward ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination").
The 997 repairs reduce to 33 root causes
(Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K The 33 root causes ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")),
almost all of them a verifier kind read two ways or a builder
instruction, so a fix made once reaches every environment that shares
it.

Figure 5: GRPO on Qwen3.8-27B with the task verifiers as a binary
reward. Left: training reward, the fraction of 96 sampled episodes the
verifier accepts. Right: AutomationBench pass rate at seven checkpoints
against the 37.6% base; from step 40 on it stays in a 38.3–41.3% band
while reward keeps climbing.

### 5.3 Replacing real atoms with generated ones

| Atoms             | AutomationBench | MCP-Mark       | BFCL v4        | env. | tokens |
|-------------------|-----------------|----------------|----------------|------|--------|
| real              | 30.3$`\pm`$0.7  | 54.9$`\pm`$2.7 | 66.3$`\pm`$0.4 | 859  | 7.6M   |
| generated data    | 28.0$`\pm`$0.9  | 51.2$`\pm`$2.8 | 65.2$`\pm`$0.4 | 759  | 7.3M   |
| generated intents | 27.3$`\pm`$0.5  | 52.4$`\pm`$2.5 | 65.9$`\pm`$0.9 | 748  | 7.4M   |

Table 3: One atom family replaced by model-generated content, the rest
fixed; Qwen3.6-27B trained on 885 trajectories per arm. Means $`\pm`$
standard deviation over four evaluations; one training run per arm.
*env.*: distinct environments among the 885 trajectories; *tokens*:
supervised tokens.

§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
varied the whole pipeline. Here we replace one atom family at a time and
keep everything else fixed: the builder and its prompt, admission, the
teacher and the acceptance rule, the length filter and the SFT recipe.
The cohort is the 1,326 environments of the round-2 sample that were
built from skeletons; the other 812 predate the skeleton of
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination").
*Real atoms* keeps their original trajectories. *Generated data*
replaces every table the builder read from a real dataset with one a
model writes from the table’s schema card (column names, types, at most
5,000 rows), without seeing a real row. *Generated intents* replaces the
3,471 mined intent atoms with ones a model writes from each server’s
capability card and the closed vocabulary of operation and verifier
kinds, without access to the mined pages; the skeletons are then
recombined to the same count with the rule atoms unchanged.

Supply falls first. The builder admits 94.3% of the generated-data
environments and 84.9% of the generated-intent ones, and the teacher
solves 67.0% and 67.8% of those at least once; the control is at 100% by
construction. The two arms end with 965 and 885 trajectories, so all
three are cut to 885 and trained alike. Real atoms lead on every suite
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Replacing real atoms with generated ones ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")):
by 2.2 and 3.0 points on AutomationBench, above its evaluation spread of
0.5–0.9; by 3.7 and 2.6 on MCP-Mark, within its spread of 2.5–2.8; and
by 1.1 and 0.4 on BFCL v4, the second within noise. Within BFCL the lead
comes from multi-turn use and irrelevance detection; the generated arms
do better on memory and web search.

Two differences in content are measured, though neither is isolated as a
cause. Generated intents shift the operations the corpus exercises:
among the 3,471 pool positions, create_record rises from 51 to 371,
delete_or_archive_row from 11 to 332, and helpdesk_reply_or_update falls
from 302 to 34. And at equal size both generated arms cover fewer
distinct environments, 759 and 748 against 859, because fewer
environments yield and more contribute a second trajectory; supervised
tokens differ by under 3.5%. Each arm is one training run, and the
MCP-Mark and BFCL v4 scores of this batch were evaluated later than
those of
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"),
so they are compared only within the table.

### 5.4 The same verifiers as a reward

Nothing is rebuilt for reinforcement learning: the verifier that
admitted an environment is the reward. We run GRPO ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21)) on the unmodified Qwen3.8-27B over 1,516
environments: those the teacher solved in one to six of eight attempts,
and the 220 it never solved, kept as an exploration set
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
profiles both). Replaying the reference solutions earns the reward; a
no-op policy does not. The pass rate moves from 37.6% into a 38.3–41.3%
band by step 40 and oscillates there
(Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 One round of evolution ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"));
every checkpoint scores above the base and, paired against it, wins more
tasks than it loses, but the margins are not significant at the 5% level
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
and no ordering inside the band is established, so we report the band,
with
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
giving one point in it. Training reward keeps rising after the pass rate
flattens: the policy goes on fitting the training environments after the
transferable part has been learned.

### 5.5 What the training does not buy

Three results go the other way or not at all. First, BFCL’s
*Irrelevance* falls by five to eight points after supervised training on
both weaker bases: every request asks for at least one write and the
negative assertions forbid particular writes, not the request as a
whole, so nothing rewards declining. Second, Qwen3.5-27B’s BFCL
multi-turn score falls from 63.3 to 54.1. Third, the MCP-Mark gain on
Qwen3.8-27B is not established: 73.2 to 77.6 against standard deviations
of 3.7 and 2.6.

## 6 Conclusion

Synthesising an agentic environment is the easy half; the hard half is
finding out that it is wrong: 28% of ours yielded no trajectory, three
quarters of those because the environment was at fault. Atoms make such
a defect attributable to a reusable unit, and a tested verifier makes a
failed rollout a bug report, not a mystery. One round of the loop raised
the yield from 71.6% to 88.3%; the environments trained three bases,
with supervised gains that transfer to MCP-Mark, outscored four public
pipelines at equal budget, and as a reward moved a strong base from
37.6% to 40.3%.

## Limitations

Four limits bound what this paper shows.

##### Scope of the comparison.

The controlled comparison of
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
covers the four public pipelines that release executable environments
with programmatic verifiers; pipelines that release only trajectories,
or whose verifier is an LLM judge, cannot be sampled by the same teacher
under the same acceptance rule, so they are compared by provenance
(Table [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"),
our reading of those papers) rather than trained on. The ablation of
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Replacing real atoms with generated ones ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
replaces the data atoms or the intent atoms with model-generated ones on
the skeleton-built part of the round-2 sample while holding the rest
fixed; each arm is one training run, so it indicates rather than
isolates the contribution of a family, and the comparison of
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
still bounds the joint effect of provenance and composition. What comes
from real sources is the atoms: the request, the verifier and the
reference solution are still written by the builder model, and the
diagnosis is made by an agent.

##### Statistical resolution.

No training run is repeated. AutomationBench scores of the models we
serve are means of one to four evaluations of 600 tasks
(Table [4](#A5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")),
so we report per-task paired counts and a band for reinforcement
learning; MCP-Mark and BFCL v4 scores are means of four evaluations
whose standard deviations reach 3.7 and 0.8 points
(Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Reasoning replay. ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")),
and we treat differences of that size as unresolved. The paired counts
of
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
point one way on every row; the closest, 69:47 for round 2 against round
1, is at the 5% level (two-sided sign test $`p\approx 0.05`$). For
reinforcement learning, one of the 18 pairings of a checkpoint
evaluation with a base evaluation is significant at that level.

##### Evaluation protocol.

Three baselines served through a commercial gateway (DeepSeek-V4-Pro,
GLM-5.2 and Kimi-K2.6, ^($`\diamond`$) in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"))
are evaluated with the model’s reasoning dropped between tool calls,
which lowers some models by several points (5.3 for Qwen3.8-27B and 6.5
for DeepSeek-V4-Flash when we measured both ways,
Table [4](#A5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
Every claim of the paper compares rows evaluated under one protocol; the
ranking of our rows against those three is not established.

##### Breadth.

Yields are given for one evolution round, on one 27B family, in English
business domains; the loop is not shown to converge.

## Appendix A The condition form

A condition is $`\langle e,\varphi,\kappa\rangle`$. The scope
$`\varphi`$ is a conjunction of clauses $`\texttt{col}\ \mathit{op}\ v`$
over 14 comparison operators (equality, order, membership, string
containment and prefix/suffix, null tests). A value $`v`$ is a literal
(a scalar or a non-scalar constant); a reference into a namespace
(\$arg, the call’s arguments; \$actor, the caller; \$session; \$now);
another column of the same row, or an arithmetic expression over such
columns; a sub-query nested at most two deep; or the value a column held
before the operation (\$was). The cardinality $`\kappa`$ is one of
$`\geq n`$, $`=n`$, $`\leq n`$, $`\neq n`$, $`>n`$, $`<n`$, with
*exists* and *not exists* as aliases. The condition appears at six sites
(read filter, entity constraint, precondition, postcondition, provides
and graph locator); each fixes which namespaces are visible, a
precondition may refer to \$arg and a verifier assertion only to the
final world, and how an undecidable comparison is treated. Guards and
verifier assertions share one representation, one operator table and one
evaluator; entity constraints and read filters use the same
representation through adapters. Over the 384 usable servers, 19,895
precondition clauses use this form.

## Appendix B Compiling a server atom

A code-reading agent is given one open-source repository and a contract
of about 1,200 lines. The contract fixes closed vocabularies for what it
may write (7 operation types, 15 effect kinds, 6 entry kinds, 3 edge
relations), gives for each a counter-example of what does not belong,
and requires absence to be stated: an empty list means “I checked”, a
missing field means “I did not look”. The agent describes every entity
with its columns and constraints, every operation with its parameters
and the effects it leaves in the database, every precondition the code
enforces and the message the code returns when it is violated, and the
relations between operations. A validator scores the description against
the contract and returns every violation, with the way to fix it, to the
same agent session, and the agent revises. Of the 467 repositories, 433
reached this stage; over four feedback rounds, 395 met the contract;
after the second stage, 384 are usable.

A second stage translates the description into an executable
specification. Everything that can be translated mechanically is, and
every default the translator had to guess is listed for the agent to
confirm; what requires reading code again, such as which entity is the
account table and which guards are real, is decided by the agent. The
runtime serves each specification as a set of tools over a relational
state, dispatching by operation family, and evaluates every precondition
through the condition form of
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A The condition form ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination").
The usable set holds 384 servers with 25,689 tools; of the 14,810 tools
with a precondition, one lacks a refusal message.

## Appendix C Atom schemas

##### Intent atom.

{app, kind, pos, neg, check_kinds}: the server (app in the skeleton
schema, service in the compiler contract); the operation kind, which
must be implemented by a write tool of that server; the number of
positive and of negative predicates the verifier should carry for this
atom (1–30 and 0–30); and the verifier kinds a verifier may use. A real
instance:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Rule atom.

{archetype, carrier, has_exception, rule_shape}. The shape is at most
400 characters and may contain no proper names and no number of two or
more digits; the validator rejects the numbers, the builder instructions
forbid the names. A real instance:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Carriers and the servers registered to host them: policy sheet
(budibase, directus, ledgersmb), policy document (outline,
paperless-ngx), policy mail (stalwart), note field (14 servers, among
them CRM, ticketing, accounting and booking applications), card
description (vikunja, mantisbt, planka), pinned channel message (zulip).

##### Data atom.

A dataset directory with a card: for each table with at least eight
rows, the type of every column (numeric, date, category, text,
identifier, contact, entity), its number of distinct values and sample
values; the rule archetypes the table can support; size and licence.

##### Server atom.

The executable specification: entities with columns and constraints,
tools with parameters, effects and preconditions in the condition form,
an account entity with a known credential, and, once onboarded, a
capability card mapping operation kinds to the tools that implement
them.

##### Skeleton.

{domain, apps, deliverable_atoms, rule_atoms, dataset_hint, n_intents,
n_distractors_min, predicate_budget, chain, source}: the business
domain; one to six servers (one to five in the corpus); the intent atoms
(deliverable_atoms in the code) and one to three rule atoms (one or two
in the corpus); the dataset, left empty when the builder is to choose
one from the pool, with schema compatibility checked then
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"));
the number of intents, the minimum number of distractor records, the
number of predicates (8–60) the verifier must at least reach, which
95.3% of skeletons do; a one-line chain from reading the carrier to the
last write; and the public URL the skeleton was mined from or the
skeleton it was recombined from. The skeleton that the two atoms above
belong to, mined from a public page on student-record rights
(bookkeeping fields omitted):

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix D Inducing the verifier kinds

To test whether the 45 verifier kinds can be recovered from public
documentation of real work, an agent on the model that builds the
environments was run over 115 public pages of business-workflow
documentation (vendor API references, help centres and procedure
documents), several sessions per page. Each session received the
condition form of
§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Shared condition form ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"),
the entity and tool metadata of the servers, and one starting page
chosen by a coordinator; for nine of the 45 kinds the coordinator also
pre-extracted public field names or schema facts from those pages. No
session received the 45 kinds or another session’s proposals; a scan of
all 5,609 input files confirms this. Each session wrote down, for the
workflow it read, what would have to hold in the final world, as a named
family with a template over the condition form, a quotation from the
source and a positive and a negative example.

Figure 6: The corpus. (a) Servers per environment; almost every
environment spans two or more. (b) Use of each server, ranked; a dozen
servers for spreadsheets, mail, chat and boards carry most of the load,
as they do in real automation templates. (c) Rule archetypes and
carriers over the 4,794 skeletons. (d) The twelve most frequent of the
110 operation kinds.

The sessions produced 1,881 family proposals, 405 of them complete.
Judged against the 45 verifier kinds, the proposals are semantically
equivalent to all 45; under a strict reading that requires the same
generic template rather than a specialisation, 3 of 45 were confirmed in
the 14 decisions reviewed, so the strict figure is a lower bound and not
an estimate. Of 64 quotations sampled across the 45 kinds, 64 were found
verbatim in the cached source page. A coordinator who knew the target
vocabulary chose the starting pages, so the result shows that the
vocabulary is recoverable from public sources given where to look, not
that it would be discovered without guidance.

##### Harness.

We run the unmodified upstream harness at version 1.0.6 on the public
split of 600 scored tasks (six domains $`\times`$ 100: Sales, Marketing,
Operations, Support, Finance, HR). Four settings matter for
comparability; we fix the hardest of the first three. (i) *Toolset*: the
api toolset, which exposes only api_search, api_fetch and base64_encode,
so the agent must discover endpoints and construct requests itself; the
benchmark’s authors report that its higher-level toolsets usually score
higher. (ii) *Step budget*: the default cap of 50 agent steps; across
the audited runs 15.9% of episodes reach it. (iii) *Coverage*: a single
rollout per task, with no best-of-$`n`$ or majority vote. (iv)
*Reasoning*: the models we serve ourselves (every LegoEnv row, its base,
and the baselines DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Flash,
HY-3 and Qwen3.5-379B) run from an inference endpoint with thinking
enabled, and the unmodified harness keeps the model’s reasoning of
earlier turns in the conversation; DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.2 and
Kimi-K2.6 are served through a commercial gateway that rejects the
reasoning of earlier turns in the request, so they receive the
conversation without it. An earlier configuration of our own gateway
dropped it too, and the paragraph *Reasoning replay* below reports both
measurements for the models we serve. We audited the graded tasks behind
24 runs under the earlier configuration and the 45 runs behind
Table [4](#A5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"):
every pass satisfies assertions_passed == assertions_total, and no
episode was aborted by the inference gateway or left with an unresolved
request fault.

##### Suites.

AutomationBench poses six domains $`\times`$ 100 tasks over simulated
SaaS applications whose REST endpoints the agent must discover, with
layered business rules and deliberately misleading records; we use the
public split, the api toolset, a cap of 50 steps per task and one
rollout, and report the official task_completed_correctly, whose mean
over tasks is the pass rate. MCP-Mark’s five servers are filesystem,
GitHub, Notion, Playwright and PostgreSQL, each task with a curated
initial state and a validation script. For BFCL v4 we report all seven
official categories (including multi-turn use and long-context memory)
and the official weighted average.

##### Checkpoint selection.

Each LegoEnv row of
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
is one checkpoint evaluated on all three suites. Qwen3.6-27B reaches
34.8% on AutomationBench with the round-3 corpus but scores lower on
MCP-Mark and BFCL v4 (59.1% and 67.9, single evaluations) than the
round-2 checkpoint in the table (68.5% and 72.4), so the table reports
the latter. For Qwen3.5-27B, the round-2 and round-3 corpora both score
26.3% against 23.2% for the round-1$`+`$3k checkpoint in the table; the
round-3 checkpoint matches it on MCP-Mark and BFCL v4 (60.6% and 67.6
over three evaluations against 60.0% and 67.6 over four), so the
ordering is not established and the table reports the checkpoint
evaluated four times. For Qwen3.8-27B, GRPO steps 200 and 240 score
40.3% and 38.3% on AutomationBench (two evaluations each; 65:53 and
56:64 per task against the first base evaluation), 77.6% and 79.5% on
MCP-Mark and 72.0 and 73.6 on BFCL v4, step 240 evaluated once there;
the MCP-Mark difference is inside the evaluation spread, the BFCL v4
difference of 1.6 favours step 240, and no ordering inside the band is
established
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 The same verifiers as a reward ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination"));
the table reports step 200, the checkpoint evaluated four times on
MCP-Mark and BFCL v4.

##### Evaluation spread.

Every model of
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
was evaluated four times on MCP-Mark and on BFCL v4 under the same
configuration, and the table reports the means;
Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Reasoning replay. ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
gives the standard deviation of the MCP-Mark pass rate and of the BFCL

Table [4](#A5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination").

##### Reasoning replay.

Served from an inference endpoint with thinking enabled, the unmodified
harness keeps the model’s reasoning of earlier turns in the
conversation; an earlier configuration of our gateway dropped it, as the
commercial gateway behind the ^($`\diamond`$) rows of
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
does.
Table [4](#A5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
reports both for every checkpoint we serve: the *dropped* column is one
evaluation each under the earlier configuration, the *replayed* column
the evaluations behind
Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
and
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination").
The bases are the most sensitive rows: Qwen3.8-27B gains 5.3 points from
the replayed reasoning and DeepSeek-V4-Flash 6.5, the two smaller bases
0.5 and 1.8. The checkpoints trained on our environments move by
$`-0.8`$ to $`+8.6`$ points and the four pipeline arms by $`-1.7`$ to
$`+0.1`$, so every supervised gain and the ordering of
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
hold under both protocols, with the lead over the closest pipeline at
3.3 points dropped and 8.0 replayed. The GRPO checkpoints, trained with
their reasoning kept, gain 0.3 to 5.2 (3.1 on average), less than their
base, so the reinforcement-learning gain is 6.2 points dropped and 2.7
replayed; of the 18 pairings of a checkpoint evaluation with a base
evaluation, 16 win more tasks than they lose, one at the 5% level (step
160 against the second base evaluation, 77:51, $`p\approx 0.03`$).
Scores in the two columns are not comparable with each other, and
neither is comparable with published numbers taken under a third
configuration.

##### Baselines.

Every baseline in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Recombination. ‣ 3.3 Structural atom recombination ‣ 3 Method ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
is an open-weight model run by us under the harness above, at its
highest available reasoning setting, five from our own endpoints and
three (^($`\diamond`$)) through a commercial inference gateway; we quote
no leaderboard numbers. Our GLM-5.2 score of 25.7% against the 26.2% on
the benchmark’s public leaderboard is a check that the configuration
reproduces the authors’.

#### Training

##### SFT.

64 H20 GPUs, 3 epochs, global batch size 32, peak learning rate
$`1\times 10^{-5}`$ with cosine decay, 64K sequence length. We export a
checkpoint at each epoch boundary and evaluate the last unless stated
otherwise. Assistant turns that receive a 4xx tool response are excluded
from the loss.

##### RL.

We run GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)) on Qwen3.8-27B,
initialised from the *unmodified* base rather than from an SFT
checkpoint, so the RL result is not confounded with the supervised one.
128 H20 GPUs (64 training, 64 rollout), group size 8, temperature 1.0, 2
epochs over 1,516 prompts, giving 252 optimisation steps ($`\approx`$34
h). The reward is exactly the task’s programmatic verifier: binary,
unshaped, with no reward model, no LLM judge and no auxiliary terms.
§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 The same verifiers as a reward ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
describes the prompt set. Of the 1,516 prompts, 536 (35.4%) exist only
because of the round-3 repairs, among them all 220 of the exploration
set. In the same teacher band (one to six successes in eight) the
repaired environments train like the native ones: over the run the
sampled reward rises from 0.40 to 0.52 for the 316 repaired environments
and from 0.48 to 0.56 for the 980 native ones, and the two curves cross
throughout
(Figure [7](#A5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ RL. ‣ Training ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
The exploration set is sampled like every other prompt (eight rollouts
per epoch, sixteen over the run): 48 of the 220 are solved at least once
during training, the first success at a median of step 91 of 252, and
172 remain unsolved at the end.

Figure 7: Training reward by prompt group during GRPO, in bins of 20
steps: the 980 native environments, the 316 repaired environments in the
same teacher band, and the 220 of the exploration set.

##### Pipeline comparison.

EnvFactory tasks are single turns of released sessions, with the session
prefix given as context and excluded from the loss (median 9 assistant
turns including the prefix); AWM trajectories are filtered by its
code-only verifier; the LLM judge of its released pipeline is not used,
and AWM’s authors report the code-only option as the weaker of the two
(Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).
All arms of
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
share the base checkpoint, learning rate, epochs, sequence length and
tool-call template; the training configurations differ only in the data
path. Trajectories are encoded with the teacher’s reasoning preserved
across turns.
Table [6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Pipeline comparison. ‣ Training ‣ Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
profiles five of them; EnvFactory’s teacher pass@8 is 0.72 over all rows
and 0.59 over the rows kept. All four pipelines are served through the
same tool interface as our environments; the mapping is structural and
changes neither tool definitions nor content. Per domain, our arm leads
AWM in all six domains (mean of four evaluations each). On the two
transfer suites our arm again ranks first: its student scores 72.4% on
MCP-Mark and 68.2 on BFCL v4, against 59.1–63.8% and 63.8–67.8 for the
four other arms, means of four evaluations
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

## Appendix F Overlap with AutomationBench

Of the transfer suites, BFCL v4 touches the corpus at one point: eight
environments (0.15%) seed the tool-catalogue table of one server from
the BFCL v3 multi-turn function catalogue, which the dataset pool held
as a public dataset; their trajectories are in the corpora of
§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
and were not removed, and the eight environments are withheld from the
public release. MCP-Mark shares no server with the pool.

AutomationBench shares no task, application or data with our
environments, and
Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix F Overlap with AutomationBench ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
measures the distance. We compare the request text of each of the 5,465
round-2 environments with the user prompt of each of the 600 public
AutomationBench tasks (their shared system prompt removed), after
lower-casing, mapping digit runs to one placeholder and stripping
punctuation. Lexical overlap is counted in shared word 13-grams and
8-grams; semantic proximity is the maximum TF-IDF cosine (sublinear tf,
smoothed idf fitted on the union of the two corpora), with the
benchmark’s own leave-one-out self-similarity as the scale. No
environment shares a 13-gram with any task. The six shared 8-grams are
ISO-8601 timestamps and the phrase “today is
$`\langle`$date$`\rangle`$”, and none remains when digits are kept.
92.0% of the benchmark tasks are closer to another benchmark task than
to any of our requests; 23 of our requests (0.4%) exceed the benchmark’s
median self-similarity and none exceeds its maximum. A dense embedding
gives the same picture: 83.5% of the benchmark tasks are closer to
another benchmark task than to any of our requests; where half of our
requests would exceed the benchmark’s median self-similarity if they
were drawn from its distribution, 0.5% do, and none reaches its maximum,
which two benchmark tasks that paraphrase each other across domains
attain. Unrelated pairs score about 0.45 in this space, so only the
comparison between the two columns carries meaning. The five nearest
pairs share a business scenario, such as invoice approval, and nothing
else. Our 223 servers are self-hosted open-source applications and the
benchmark’s 47 are simulated commercial SaaS tools; the two sets are
disjoint, and the benchmark’s worlds are synthetic. The benchmark places
the governing rule in a record of the environment rather than in the
prompt in 44.5% of its tasks, so the request-level comparison is like
for like.

| Measure | ours vs. AB | AB vs. itself |
|----|----|----|
| sharing a 13-gram | 0 / 5,465 (0.0%) | 351 / 600 (58.5%) |
| sharing an 8-gram | 81 / 5,465 (1.5%)^($`\ast`$) | 401 / 600 (66.8%) |
| TF-IDF max cosine, median | 0.198 | 0.344 |
| TF-IDF max cosine, max | 0.442 | 0.680 |
| embedding max cosine, median | 0.719 | 0.779 |
| embedding max cosine, max | 0.930 | 0.965 |
| applications in common | 0 of 223 vs. 47 | — |

## Appendix G Corpus profile

Figure [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Inducing the verifier kinds ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
profiles the 5,465 environments of the round-2 corpus by servers per
environment, server frequency, rule archetypes and carriers, and
operation kinds.

The round-2 corpus is 6,110 trajectories over 5,465 environments drawing
on 223 distinct applications. A trajectory spans 2.51 applications on
average (median 2; 1/2/3/4/5 applications in 31/3,361/2,359/315/44
trajectories), so 99.5% of the corpus is cross-application; the
distribution is long-tailed but not degenerate, with the ten most
frequent applications accounting for 60.6% of application slots (58.8%
counted per environment,
Figure [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Inducing the verifier kinds ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")b)
and the most frequent single one for 15.2%. Each task carries a verifier
of 13.1 clauses on average (median 13, p90 24, max 54) and a gold
witness of 12.2 actions (median 10, p90 25, max 64). The trajectories
themselves run 14.8 assistant turns (median 13, p90 26, max 70) and
19,784 tokens (median 18,504, max 65,498); 33.3% of the 120.9M tokens
carry loss, and 23.4% of trajectories contain at least one 4xx tool
response, whose turns are masked out of the loss
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Experimental details ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")).

## Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from

Table [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I Where the content of related environments comes from ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
reads the pipelines of
§[2](#S2 "2 Related Work ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
part by part: EnvScaler ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)),
AgentScaler ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)), TOUCAN ([Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)), Agent-World ([Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)),
AWM ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib5)), ScaleEnv ([Tu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)), AgentSkiller ([Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)),
EnvFactory ([Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib3)), C-World ([Xi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)), AutoForge ([Cai et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)),
COVERT ([Xu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib14)), EnvCraft ([Zeng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)), CompoWorld ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib38)). Every
cell was checked against the full text of the paper. Two pipelines,
TOUCAN and C-World, execute real remote services, so their tools and
returned data are real, but they fix no initial state, cannot reset a
task, and train by supervised fine-tuning only. EnvFactory and
CompoWorld start from real tool interfaces (API documentation, crawled
MCP specifications) and have an agent write the implementation, the
schema and the data; EnvCraft starts from community scenario names and
generates the rest. Agent-World mines part of its databases from the web
and extends them with generated rows. AWM’s released pipeline offers a
code-only verifier beside its default code-plus-judge one; its authors
report the code-only option as the weaker of the two, and it is the one
the arm of
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Environments from other pipelines ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
uses.

Table 12: Ten sources. Template, documentation and procedure rows give
the rule atom (archetype, carrier) and the intents (kind on server) of
the skeleton mined from the page; dataset rows give the dataset card’s
domain and columns; repository rows give the server atom compiled from
the code.

##### A server atom.

Figure [10](#A11.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix K The 33 root causes ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")
shows the repair of the wiki server raneto. Its search tool was a
keyword search, but the runtime’s keyword executor reads only the
arguments q and query while the tool’s argument is search, so every
query returned an empty list. Its edit and delete tools located a page
by filepath, whose seeded values carry the .md extension, while the
argument description asks for a path without it, so a call made as
described failed with “page does not exist”. Categories and page
metadata were readable by no tool. The repair makes search a substring
filter over title and body, locates pages by slug, makes the page read
public with its metadata, requires a category on page creation, and adds
two list tools; the server goes from 10 to 12 tools.

##### An environment.

In bozeman_remodel, the request allows a remodel work log per property,
but the verifier required all four property names in one document. The
repair accepts either one merged log or one log per property and keeps
the requirement that every property is covered.

##### Operation kinds.

Two counts describe the operation kinds. The registered vocabulary grew
with onboarding in three steps
(Table [11](#A12.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix L Repair examples ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")):
31 to 37 kinds with six servers (19 to 25), 37 to 57 with seven servers
(25 to 32), and a final classification of all 3,935 historical write
steps that kept a new kind only where no existing one fit, 110 in all.
The order in which servers were onboarded was computed, not chosen: each
candidate is ranked by how often mining named it before it was
onboarded. The counts of
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environmentsvia Modular Recombination")b,
81, 91 and 109, are the kinds observed in each round’s writes and
skeletons under that final taxonomy (81 counts the 1,166 of 1,204
round-0 environments the atomisation covers); round 1 adds ten. Kinds
enter the vocabulary when a skeleton needs them: three mined
government-domain skeletons named ckan’s dataset_publish and
dataset_metadata_patch, which the validator rejected as kind not in
vocab; onboarding ckan added both kinds and resource_publish, and the
skeletons then passed. The taxonomy was also corrected after the fact: a
Bitwarden call organizationuser_update with a Type argument, first
classed as manage_membership_or_invitation, was moved to
manage_role_or_permission because Type is the role field, while calls
that change only Status stayed.
````
